Ok, so I've played Eve, and I have to tell you that it is by far the most ambitious game I have ever seen. You can do almost anything you want. The tutorials in the beginning of the game are meant to help you decide what type of role you want to fulfill in the universe. They give you a small taste of the things you can do in the hopes that you will figure the rest out on your own. Their is a common joke about the Eve learning curve that usually manifests in this ---> http://i.imgur.com/jj16ThL.jpg

Also, if you are trying to play the game all alone you are going to have a bad time. It's meant to be played with a group, called a Corp. These Corps hold down space, fulfill trade rolls, mine for resources, serve as mercenaries, or become pirates. It's all about what you want to do. If you want to find a corp, I would suggest checking out Brave Newbies or Eve Academy. They are both designed to help new players, and Eve Academy is specifically designed to teach.

Most of the time if you are in a corp of sufficient size, you have near unlimited access to the Tier 1 Frigates. Use these to learn every game mechanic you can keep in your skull. There is a lot to this game and being good at it takes time, research, dedication, and work. However it is one of the most fulfilling experiences in gaming I've ever found. It really makes you feel like you are out there, and if you are alone, you are a real small fish, in an ocean of predators.

PVP is non consensual in low-sec and in null-sec. You can and will be killed. You will die, and you will die a lot. It's kind of like Dota or Dark Souls in that everyone sucks when they start, everyone. If you don't stay in high sec, which I suggest you leave as soon as you find a corp you like, regardless of how large of a group you are traveling with, you are at risk. You must pay attention, keep your head on a swivel, and be careful, from un-dock, to dock.

The skill system in Eve demands dedication due to training in real time. You will inevitably gain the ability to fly ships far before you should, and you will lose ships precious to you, in both sentimental and resource value. Support skills are a huge factor in your stats. This is why it's best to stick to the frigs for a while until you have the support skills you need to be effective in larger ships.

The game isn't for everyone and even long time players are reffered to as Bitter Vets, but it is an experience that will almost certainly leave a unique impact on you. If you have just started, I would say run the trial to it's end with the purpose of finding something you really like doing. If you don't, don't play, if you do, watch your six and fly safe.

The first thing you have to realize is that EVE Online is actually a very shitty game if you play solo, and this is because EVE is a true multiplayer game. If you really want to enjoy the game to it's fullest, download TS3 or Mumble and join one of the active instructional corporations - of which EVE University is the most prominent. You can sample almost every playstyle in "the Uni" and decide what you like while you learn about it. After you've got a good grasp on it, you can then "graduate" into a "real" corp in HiSec, LowSec, NullSec, or my favorite space: Wormholes. I would suggest avoiding HiSec corps as most are shit and don't even use VOIP. LowSec is a lot of fun, especially if you join a militia ("factional warfare"). FW allows you to make ISK while learning PvP and building a network of contacts. You can also join NullSec, although for a months-old newbie living out there can be pretty hard. WH's are also off the table for a while as you don't have the SP for it (it's much higher end gameplay, using specialized tech2 and tech3 ships of which you need to be able to fly a variety of).

I've played the game for 6 years, and yes, I also struggled in the beginning. I almost quit several times. The first month is honestly the hardest. But it's the people I play with that kept me playing. And I learn new things about the game almost every day, even after 6 years.
